message.content:
Nxeon platform (/opt/nxeon), a VPS/game hosting business with a live-chat AI support widget. The chat agent (`lib/kb-llm.ts` → `lib/kb.ts` → `lib/kb-run.ts`) answers strictly from a knowledge base string in `lib/kb-system.ts` (`KB_SYSTEM`), which its own system prompt calls "the assistant's authoritative source of truth" and instructs it to "answer ONLY from the facts in this document" — i.e. it deliberately does NOT invent or guess about features not documented there. `KB_PAGES` (same file or a sibling, check) is a list of real dashboard routes it can link customers to. `lib/kb-plans.ts` holds structured plan/pricing cards it can render.

A real customer just asked "how do I get a free minecraft server" and the chat agent wrongly said no free option exists — root cause (already found and FIXED in a prior pass, commit `dad7b9c05b`, already deployed to production): the free Minecraft tier (`freemc-host`, shipped 2026-08-24) was never added to `KB_SYSTEM`/`KB_PAGES`/`KB_PLANS` because it shipped as a separate initiative from the normal paid-catalog seed sources that `KB_SYSTEM` has a maintained mapping-comment tracking.

The owner has now explicitly asked to "go deep into all of the automated responses and update them and add more if necessary as we have added a lot more" — i.e. a full audit, not just the one gap. The same prior investigation already spotted (but didn't fix) more of the same pattern: `lib/nx/nav.ts` itself has comments flagging past "real feature, no way to reach it" fixes for these real, live routes that are currently MISSING from `KB_PAGES`: `/dashboard/build` (Matrix/Build-with-AI console), `/dashboard/partner` (Partner Program), `/dashboard/tools` (consolidated Tools hub), `/dashboard/directory` (in-portal Server Directory), `/dashboard/whats-new`.

YOUR TASK — go deep, comprehensively:

1. Read `lib/kb-system.ts` in full to understand its structure (the sections, the "seed source" mapping comment convention, how it's organized by product line) and `lib/kb-plans.ts` and wherever `KB_PAGES` actually lives.
2. Read `lib/nx/nav.ts` in full — it's evidently already a maintained, authoritative list of every real customer-facing route/feature in the product, given it has its own history of "real feature, no way to reach it" fixes noted in comments. Use it as your primary cross-reference ground truth for "what real things exist that a customer could ask about."
3. For EVERY real feature/route you find in nav.ts (and anywhere else customer-facing — check `app/dashboard/` route folders directly too, as a second cross-check, in case something exists but isn't even in nav.ts), verify it's accurately and adequately represented in `KB_SYSTEM` (does the chat agent know what it does, who it's for, how to access it) AND in `KB_PAGES` (can the chat agent actually link to it). Build a concrete checklist and go through it methodically — don't sample, cover all of it. Categories to make sure you cover: VPS hosting, all game server families and any recent additions, the free Minecraft tier, shared hosting (check its current enabled/inert status — don't advertise it as live if it's still gated behind ENABLE_SHARED_HOSTING and inert), NxCloud, Kodely SSO/partner integration, the referral/affiliate program, domain registration, email/mailboxes, backups/malware-scanner add-ons, dedicated IP add-on, disk expansion, 2FA/security settings, the Matrix/Build-with-AI console, the Partner Program, the Tools hub, the Server Directory, What's New, migration tools, win-back/promo codes, wallet/billing/invoices, support tickets, the grandfather pricing program (should the chat agent be able to explain to a customer why their renewal price differs from the current catalog price, if asked?), the new intro-price/discount-badge pricing display (if a customer asks "why does the checkout price differ from what support told me," does the chat agent's knowledge match the current real pricing mechanism?).
4. For every genuine gap found, fix it: add the missing route to `KB_PAGES`, add accurate prose to the correct `KB_SYSTEM` section (matching its existing style/structure — check the "seed source" mapping comment convention and add a note for anything you add so this doesn't drift again), and add a plan/pricing card to `kb-plans.ts` if that's the established pattern for a product line (check how existing product lines like VPS/game/free-MC now do it, for consistency).
5. Do NOT touch anything that's correctly and deliberately absent (e.g., if shared hosting really is inert/unlaunched, the chat agent should say so honestly or not offer to sell it — don't make it falsely claim it's available; verify current real status via the actual feature flag/env var before writing anything).
6. IMPORTANT — credential hygiene: a prior pass in this exact investigation accidentally printed the production database password to its own transcript log by running `cat .env | grep DATABASE_URL` directly. Do NOT do this. If you need to query the live DB read-only, use this repo's established convention: write a `.ts` script under `/opt/nxeon/scripts/_tmp-*.ts` that imports `db` from `../lib/db` (the Prisma client, which reads its own connection config internally) and run it via `npx tsx scripts/_tmp-whatever.ts` from within `/opt/nxeon` — never construct or print a raw `psql`/`DATABASE_URL` connection string yourself. Delete the temp script when done.
7. Test the fixes for real: invoke the actual `kbAnswer()` (or whatever the real chat-agent entry point is, check `test/chat-agent-tools.test.ts` for the existing pattern) with a handful of realistic customer questions covering several of the newly-added areas (e.g. "what's the partner program", "how do I use the AI build console", "can I see other people's public servers", "why is my renewal price different from what's on the pricing page now") and confirm accurate, non-hallucinated answers that match real current functionality.
8. Deploy through the normal pipeline: commit → push → deploy-staging.sh → verify HTTP 200 → promote-production.sh → verify HTTP 200 AND a genuinely fresh BUILD_ID (compare against the current value first, don't trust a stale-looking match). Note: another background process may have landed an unrelated commit on production very recently (a dashboard "Resource Usage widget" fix, commit `bc2a67626b` or later) — that's expected and fine, just make sure your own commit is included in whatever you promote, don't revert or conflict with it.

Do NOT reply to any customer or ticket — this is purely a knowledge-base code fix.

Report back concisely: the full checklist of what you audited, exactly what gaps you found and fixed (route + KB_SYSTEM + KB_PLANS as applicable, per item), what you deliberately left alone as correctly-not-yet-launched, your test results, and confirmation of production deploy with a fresh BUILD_ID.

1	/* The sidebar, exactly as the design has it — the same six groups, the same
2	   twelve items, the same icons and badges. Only the hrefs differ from the
3	   sandbox's, because here they point at the real route tree.
4	
5	   The live portal ships a much longer flat rail. Anything not in this list is
6	   still reachable by URL; it just isn't in the designed navigation yet. Add a
7	   row here when a screen graduates into the design. */
8	
9	export type NavItem = {
10	  group: string;
11	  label: string;
12	  icon: string;
13	  href: string;
14	  badge?: string;
15	};
16	
17	export const NAV: NavItem[] = [
18	  { group: "Overview", label: "Dashboard", icon: "home", href: "/dashboard" },
19	  { group: "Compute", label: "Deploy", icon: "cloudup", href: "/dashboard/deploy" },
20	  /* The consolidated estate view. It REPLACED the three per-product rails
21	     (Servers / Hosting / Game servers) rather than sitting beside them: those
22	     pages are still live and still where you manage one service, but they are
23	     now reached by opening a card, the way a detail page should be. Carrying
24	     both would have meant four rail entries listing overlapping subsets of the
25	     same account. See SERVICE_DETAIL_PREFIXES below for how they stay lit. */
26	  { group: "Compute", label: "My Services", icon: "cube", href: "/dashboard/services", badge: "FREE" },
27	  { group: "Build", label: "Matrix", icon: "terminal", href: "/dashboard/build", badge: "AI" },
28	  /* /dashboard/claude-code had no rail entry either — the whole starter-prompt
29	     library, the sign-in walkthrough and the guides were reachable only by
30	     typing the URL or following a cross-link from Matrix. Same "real feature,
31	     no way to reach it" shape as Migration and Tools. */
32	  { group: "Build", label: "Build with AI", icon: "sparkles", href: "/dashboard/claude-code" },
33	  /* Migration had NO rail entry at all — the page, the wizard and the whole
34	     real engine behind it were reachable only by typing the URL. Tools was in
35	     the same shape before it was added here: sixteen working tools on a page
36	     nothing linked to. They share a group because they are the same kind of
37	     thing — utilities you visit for a job, not services you own. */
38	  { group: "Tools", label: "Migration", icon: "transfer2", href: "/dashboard/migrate" },
39	  { group: "Tools", label: "Tools", icon: "sliders", href: "/dashboard/tools" },
40	  /* The directory was a link OUT to the marketing site, so browsing servers
41	     meant leaving the product and landing somewhere that knew nothing about
42	     you. It is a real page now, and it belongs here for the same reason the
43	     other two do: a job you visit, not a service you own. */
44	  { group: "Tools", label: "Server Directory", icon: "globe3", href: "/dashboard/directory" },
45	  { group: "Network", label: "Domains", icon: "nodes", href: "/dashboard/domains" },
46	  { group: "Network", label: "SSL", icon: "lock2", href: "/dashboard/ssl" },
47	  /* TWO pages, not one. `/dashboard/email` is Business Email — the plan and
48	     mailbox management screen, where checkout fulfilment lands and where search,
49	     the DNS setup flow and the hosting Email tab all link. `/dashboard/mail` is
50	     the Inbox (webmail). This rail carried a single "Mailboxes" entry pointing
51	     at the INBOX, so after paying for email a customer landed on a page the
52	     navigation could not get them back to. */
53	  { group: "Mail", label: "Mailboxes", icon: "envelope", href: "/dashboard/email" },
54	  { group: "Mail", label: "Inbox", icon: "inbox", href: "/dashboard/mail" },
55	  /* /refer and /affiliate were separate rails for the same casual
56	     referral programme — one entry for both, as before.
57	     /dashboard/partner used to be folded into this one too, on the reasoning
58	     that it only showed anything to an account that already was a partner —
59	     which also meant an account that WASN'T yet had no way to discover the
60	     programme existed at all. Rebuilt against the board's Partner.png concept
61	     with a real pitch for that case (real commission tiers, an apply path),
62	     so it earns its own entry now — same "real feature, no way to reach it"
63	     fix as Tools got. */
64	  { group: "Account", label: "Refer & earn", icon: "handshake", href: "/dashboard/refer" },
65	  { group: "Account", label: "Partner Program", icon: "layers", href: "/dashboard/partner" },
66	  { group: "Account", label: "Team", icon: "users2", href: "/dashboard/team" },
67	  { group: "Account", label: "Billing", icon: "card", href: "/dashboard/billing" },
68	  { group: "Account", label: "Activity", icon: "activity", href: "/dashboard/activity" },
69	  { group: "Account", label: "What's New", icon: "sparkles", href: "/dashboard/whats-new" },
70	  { group: "Account", label: "Support", icon: "lifebuoy", href: "/dashboard/support" },
71	  { group: "Account", label: "Settings", icon: "gear", href: "/dashboard/settings" },
72	];
73	
74	/**
75	 * Which nav item should be highlighted for a path.
76	 *
77	 * The rail used to test each item with `path === href || path.startsWith(href + "/")`
78	 * independently, which lit up TWO items on every page below the root: "Dashboard"
79	 * is `/dashboard`, and `/dashboard/servers` starts with `/dashboard/`, so Dashboard
80	 * stayed selected no matter where you were.
81	 *
82	 * Longest match wins instead, so the most specific item — and only that one — is
83	 * active. Returns null when the path is outside the rail entirely.
84	 */
85	/**
86	 * Routes that have no rail entry of their own but belong under one.
87	 *
88	 * The per-product pages left the rail when My Services replaced them, and
89	 * without this a customer who opened a server would watch the highlight jump
90	 * to "Dashboard" — the longest-match rule below would find only `/dashboard`.
91	 * These are the detail pages you reach FROM a service card, so they light the
92	 * card's own entry.
93	 */
94	const NAV_ALIASES: { prefix: string; href: string }[] = [
95	  { prefix: "/dashboard/servers", href: "/dashboard/services" },
96	  { prefix: "/dashboard/hosting", href: "/dashboard/services" },
97	  { prefix: "/dashboard/games", href: "/dashboard/services" },
98	  { prefix: "/dashboard/free-minecraft", href: "/dashboard/services" },
99	];
100	
101	export function activeNavHref(path: string): string | null {
102	  let best: string | null = null;
103	  for (const n of NAV) {
104	    if (path === n.href || path.startsWith(n.href + "/")) {
105	      if (!best || n.href.length > best.length) best = n.href;
106	    }
107	  }
108	  for (const a of NAV_ALIASES) {
109	    if (path === a.prefix || path.startsWith(a.prefix + "/")) {
110	      // An alias is always more specific than the `/dashboard` root it would
111	      // otherwise lose to, and never overrides a real entry that matched.
112	      if (!best || best.length <= "/dashboard".length) best = a.href;
113	    }
114	  }
115	  return best;
116	}

600	/** Read one setting, falling back to an explicit default then SETTINGS_DEFAULTS. */
601	export async function getSetting(key: SettingKey | string, fallback?: string): Promise<string> {
602	  const row = await db.setting.findUnique({ where: { key } });
603	  if (row) return row.value;
604	  return fallback ?? SETTINGS_DEFAULTS[key as SettingKey] ?? "";
605	}

1	/**
2	 * VPS INTRO PRICING — a LOW first-term price that RENEWS at the regular price
3	 * (classic hosting promo: "$3.99/mo first term, renews at $6.49/mo").
4	 *
5	 * This is deliberately modelled as a FIRST-TERM-ONLY discount so it rides the
6	 * plumbing the platform already has, rather than adding a second renewal price:
7	 *
8	 *   - The ORDER (lib/order.ts) charges the intro-reduced first term and stamps the
9	 *     implied first-term rate on `Server.termPromoPercent` (the very column every
10	 *     later proration/refund already prices against — see lib/proration.ts).
11	 *   - RENEWAL (lib/renewal-charge.ts — the SINGLE renewal formula) reads
12	 *     `plan.priceCents` and knows NOTHING about `introPriceCents`, so a renewal is
13	 *     billed at the regular price by construction. No renewal code changes.
14	 *
15	 * Pure & deterministic (no `db`, no I/O), so it can be imported by the order core,
16	 * the marketing pricing cards and unit tests alike. The two READERS below cast to
17	 * reach `introPriceCents` / `introTermMonths` because the symlinked prod Prisma
18	 * client's types predate these columns until it is regenerated at deploy — the
19	 * same stale-client gap `frozenProductAnnualPct` (lib/product-billing.ts) and the
20	 * `Server` writes in lib/order.ts already work around. Identical at runtime once
21	 * the client is regenerated.
22	 */
23	import { termDiscountPct } from "./billing-terms";
24	
25	/** A row that MAY carry the intro columns (present at runtime, absent from stale types). */
26	type PlanIntroFields = { introPriceCents?: number | null; introTermMonths?: number | null };
27	
28	/**
29	 * The plan's intro MONTHLY price in cents, or null when it is unset, malformed, or
30	 * NOT genuinely below the regular price. Requiring `intro < regular` means a bad /
31	 * equal / higher value can never quietly RAISE the first-term charge — it just
32	 * disables the intro and the plan bills its regular price.
33	 *
34	 * `plan` is typed loose on the intro column because the symlinked prod Prisma client's
35	 * types predate it (regenerated at deploy); the value is present at runtime.
36	 */
37	export function planIntroMonthlyCents(plan: { priceCents: number }): number | null {
38	  const v = (plan as PlanIntroFields).introPriceCents;
39	  if (typeof v !== "number" || !Number.isFinite(v) || v < 0) return null;
40	  const cents = Math.round(v);
41	  if (cents >= plan.priceCents) return null;
42	  return cents;
43	}
44	
45	/**
46	 * How many of the first term's months are billed at the intro rate. NULL / invalid
47	 * => the WHOLE first term (returned as null so callers apply it across every month).
48	 * Clamped to >= 1 so a stray 0 can never zero the intro window. `plan` is `unknown`
49	 * for the same stale-client reason as above.
50	 */
51	export function planIntroTermMonths(plan: unknown): number | null {
52	  const v = (plan as PlanIntroFields | null | undefined)?.introTermMonths;
53	  if (typeof v !== "number" || !Number.isFinite(v) || v < 1) return null;
54	  return Math.round(v);
55	}
56	
57	/**
58	 * Cents knocked off the FIRST term because of the intro rate — 0 when there is no
59	 * intro. Expressed as a REDUCTION of the regular term total (not a second price)
60	 * so the regular term price stays the single source of truth and the renewal math
61	 * is untouched:
62	 *
63	 *   discount = (regularMonthly − introMonthly) × introMonths × (1 − termDiscount)
64	 *
65	 * `introMonths` is `min(introTermMonths ?? months, months)`, so a 1-month term is
66	 * fully intro-priced, and a "$3.99 first month" intro on a 12-month first order
67	 * discounts exactly one month and bills the other eleven at the regular rate.
68	 * The term discount is applied so the intro months are discounted consistently
69	 * with the rest of the term the customer chose.
70	 */
71	export function introFirstTermDiscountCents(
72	  regularMonthlyCents: number,
73	  introMonthlyCents: number | null,
74	  termMonths: number,
75	  introTermMonths: number | null,
76	  annualDiscountPct?: number,
77	): number {
78	  if (introMonthlyCents == null || introMonthlyCents >= regularMonthlyCents) return 0;
79	  const months = Math.max(1, Math.round(termMonths));
80	  const introMonths = introTermMonths != null ? Math.min(introTermMonths, months) : months;
81	  if (introMonths <= 0) return 0;
82	  const pct = termDiscountPct(months, annualDiscountPct);
83	  return Math.max(0, Math.round((regularMonthlyCents - introMonthlyCents) * introMonths * (1 - pct / 100)));
84	}
85	
86	/**
87	 * The percent OFF the regular term total that the intro first term represents,
88	 * as a whole number 0..100 — the value stamped on `Server.termPromoPercent` so
89	 * proration and refunds price against the rate the term was actually sold at.
90	 * Integer because it round-trips through Stripe metadata as an integer promo
91	 * percent (lib/order.ts parseOrderPrice), exactly like the seasonal promos.
92	 */
93	export function introSoldPercent(regularTermCents: number, introDiscountCents: number): number {
94	  if (regularTermCents <= 0 || introDiscountCents <= 0) return 0;
95	  return Math.min(100, Math.max(0, Math.round((introDiscountCents / regularTermCents) * 100)));
96	}

content.content:
=== Q: What's the partner program? Is it different from the referral program?
kind: answer | cardKeys: undefined
A: Yes, totally different programs with different payouts.

**Refer & Earn** (/dashboard/refer): casual, self-serve. You share a link, earn a flat wallet credit per paying friend who signs up — $5/referral at the starter tier, $8 at Pro (5+ referrals), $12 at Elite (15+). It's quick money but one-time per person.

**Partner Program** (/dashboard/partner): bigger deal. You get a LIFETIME percentage commission on everything a referred customer ever spends — their first order AND every renewal after, for as long as they stay. Tiers start at 10% (Starter), 15% (Growth), 20% (Pro), and up to Custom rates for larger partners. But it's not self-serve signup — you apply via the page and a human sets it up, usually for agencies, creators, communities, developers, or resellers bringing in real volume.

TL;DR: Refer & Earn is "share a link, get $5 per friend." Partner is "bring us serious business, get 10–20% of their lifetime spend."

=== Q: How do I use the AI build console / Matrix thing?
kind: answer | cardKeys: undefined
A: Matrix is the live AI build/terminal workspace inside your dashboard — you can describe a site or app in plain English and Claude builds it for you, or drop to a raw terminal if you want to code/SSH into it yourself.

Here's the flow: head to **/dashboard/claude-code** first — that's got the starter-prompt library, a sign-in walkthrough, and guides to get you oriented. Once you've looked at those, jump into **/dashboard/build** to open the live Matrix console. From there you chat with the AI, upload files if you need to, use live voice dictation, and it builds while you watch. If the AI-assisted path isn't what you want, you can drop to a raw terminal and run commands directly.

It runs on your VPS or hosting and works with a Claude subscription or your own API key. What kind of site or app are you thinking of building?

=== Q: Can I see other people's public Minecraft servers?
kind: answer | cardKeys: undefined
A: Yes — sign in and go to the Server Directory at /dashboard/directory. You can browse other customers' public Minecraft servers by family, region, and live player count. Only servers their owner chose to list publicly show up, and you only see the name, description, and connection address they shared — never their identity or raw IP.

[[cards: game-minecraft-free]]

=== Q: Why is my renewal price different from what's on the pricing page now?
kind: answer | cardKeys: undefined
A: Good question — it's actually by design. When you signed up, your VPS/game server locked in the price you were sold at, and that rate stays with your server for as long as you keep it, even if we change the plan price on the pricing page later (up or down). It's price protection.

So your renewal bill shows what you originally paid for, not today's catalog number. You can check your exact renewal amount anytime at /dashboard/billing or /dashboard/invoices — that's your locked rate. Sound right, or does something look off?

=== Q: Can I sign up for NxCloud right now?
kind: answer | cardKeys: undefined
A: Not quite — NxCloud is real and the plans are solid, but ordering is currently gated pending some backend work. You can see the plans ($5.99/mo for Personal up to $34.99/mo for Business with Collabora Office + Talk), but there's no live Launch button yet.

Best move: head to /dashboard/nxcloud and join the waitlist so you get notified the moment it opens. Or I can connect you with a human if you want more details on what's coming.

=== Q: Does the VPS come with malware scanning or Docker?
kind: answer | cardKeys: undefined
A: Both are FREE add-ons you can toggle on at deploy time — they're not baked into every VPS by default. During the Deploy wizard, there's an Add-ons step where you pick:
- **Malware scanner (ClamAV)** — blocks malicious files and suspicious activity
- **Docker manager** — Docker + Compose preinstalled to run containers instantly

Once you launch the server, those toggles lock in and can't be changed from the dashboard afterward, so pick what you want upfront. If you need to add or remove them later, support can help.

Which VPS size are you eyeing?

=== Q: What's new in the dashboard lately?
kind: answer | cardKeys: undefined
A: The actual product update log lives in your dashboard at **/dashboard/whats-new** — that's the real, live changelog of what's shipped recently. You can also toggle your email preferences there if you want notifications on future updates.

Want me to point you at anything specific that's come out, or do you need to sign in first?

# Deploy a ref (default: main from /opt/nxeon) to the staging environment.
# Usage: ./scripts/deploy-staging.sh [git-ref]
set -euo pipefail
REF="${1:-main}"
cd /opt/nxeon-staging

git fetch origin
git reset --hard "origin/$REF"

echo "==> Installing dependencies"
npm install --no-audit --no-fund 2>&1 | tail -1

echo "==> Applying database schema"
npx prisma db push --accept-data-loss 2>&1 | tail -2
npm run db:seed 2>&1 | tail -2 || true

echo "==> Building"
npm run build 2>&1 | tail -4

# next.config sets output:"standalone" but the systemd unit runs the standalone
# server.js directly (not `next start`, which Next.js explicitly does not
# support alongside output:"standalone" — it prints a warning and silently
# fails to resolve some routes, confirmed live 2026-09-10: a brand-new API
# route 404'd under `next start` on this exact build and returned 200 under
# `node .next/standalone/server.js`). The standalone output does NOT include
# public/ or .next/static/ (Next's own documented behavior) — copy them in
# fresh every build, or every static asset/route added after the last copy
# is missing until the next deploy happens to also touch this step.
echo "==> Copying static assets into the standalone server output"
rm -rf .next/standalone/public .next/standalone/.next/static

# Web runs as the unprivileged 'nxeon' user. Only .next needs to be writable by
# it (Next cache); the rest stays root-owned and world-readable, and systemd
# injects .env as root. Do NOT chown the whole tree (breaks root git on .git).
echo "==> Fixing .next ownership for non-root web"
chown -R nxeon:nxeon /opt/nxeon-staging/.next 2>/dev/null || true
chmod 600 /opt/nxeon-staging/.env 2>/dev/null || true

echo "==> Restarting staging services"
systemctl restart nxeon-staging-web nxeon-staging-worker
sleep 5
systemctl is-active nxeon-staging-web nxeon-staging-worker
CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://127.0.0.1:8080/)
echo "==> Staging responds: HTTP $CODE (http://$(grep ^PUBLIC_IP .env | cut -d= -f2):8080)"
[ "$CODE" = "200" ] || { echo "STAGING UNHEALTHY"; exit 1; }
echo "==> Staging deploy complete"

#!/bin/bash
# Promote the currently deployed staging commit to production.
# Verifies staging is healthy, fast-forwards nothing (prod working tree IS the repo),
# then rebuilds + restarts production services.
set -euo pipefail

STG_COMMIT=$(git -C /opt/nxeon-staging rev-parse HEAD)
PROD_COMMIT=$(git -C /opt/nxeon rev-parse HEAD)

echo "==> Staging is at:    $STG_COMMIT"
echo "==> Production is at: $PROD_COMMIT"

if ! systemctl is-active -q nxeon-staging-web; then
  echo "Refusing to promote: staging web service is not running." >&2
  exit 1
fi
CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://127.0.0.1:8080/)
if [ "$CODE" != "200" ]; then
  echo "Refusing to promote: staging returns HTTP $CODE." >&2
  exit 1
fi

if [ "$STG_COMMIT" != "$PROD_COMMIT" ]; then
  echo "Note: production tree is at a different commit than staging."
  echo "Production deploys directly from /opt/nxeon's working tree (main)."
fi

cd /opt/nxeon
echo "==> Installing dependencies (adds any new deps before build)"
# CRITICAL: without this, a commit that adds a new dependency (e.g. imapflow)
# builds against a stale node_modules and fails — which previously aborted the
# promote AFTER the old build was already gone. Always sync deps first.
npm install --no-audit --no-fund 2>&1 | tail -3
# CRITICAL: this was previously `prisma generate` only — regenerates the
# CLIENT's types (fixes the build) but never touches the actual DATABASE.
# Staging and production are SEPARATE databases (nxeon_staging vs nxeon, same
# Postgres server, confirmed live) — deploy-staging.sh's own `db push` only
# ever applies to staging's DB, so a schema change promoted this way built
# and deployed fine while production's actual table never got the new
# column, silently breaking the FIRST thing that queried it post-deploy
# (found live 2026-09-02: worker/billing.ts's sweeps started throwing
# "column does not exist" immediately after a routine promote — no staging
# failure gave any warning, since staging's own db push had already
# succeeded there). `db push` both applies the schema AND regenerates the
# client, so this replaces the old generate-only step rather than adding a
# second one. Schema changes are rare enough that this always running
# unconditionally costs nothing when there's nothing new to push.
echo "==> Applying database schema"
npx prisma db push --accept-data-loss --schema=/opt/nxeon/prisma/schema.prisma 2>&1 | tail -4
echo "==> Building production"
npm run build 2>&1 | tail -4
# Guard: never restart into an incomplete/failed build. A valid production build
# always writes .next/BUILD_ID; if it's missing the build failed mid-way and the
# old in-memory process is still serving — abort rather than kill it.
if [ ! -s /opt/nxeon/.next/BUILD_ID ]; then
  echo "BUILD FAILED: .next/BUILD_ID missing — NOT restarting (old process left serving)." >&2
  exit 1
fi
# next.config sets output:"standalone"; the standalone server.js is what the
# systemd unit actually runs (not `next start` — see deploy-staging.sh's own
# comment on this same step for the 2026-09-10 incident). Its output does NOT
# include public/ or .next/static/ (Next's documented behavior) — refresh
# them every promote, same as staging, or new/changed static assets are
# missing from prod until the next promote happens to also touch this step.
echo "==> Copying static assets into the standalone server output"
rm -rf .next/standalone/public .next/standalone/.next/static
cp -r public .next/standalone/public
cp -r .next/static .next/standalone/.next/static
# geoip-lite is in next.config.ts's serverExternalPackages (kept OUT of the JS
# bundle since it reads .dat files off its own package path at runtime) — the
# standalone output tracer only copies files it can trace as JS-imported, so
# an externalized package's own non-JS data files are silently left behind.
# Found live 2026-09-10 on staging: this crashes EVERY request with an
# uncaught ENOENT the moment something runs the standalone server.js instead
# of `next start` — geo-ip.ts's own try/catch around geoip.lookup() does NOT
# help, the failure isn't confined to that call. Copy the real data/
# directory every promote, same reasoning as public/.next/static above. This
# has NOT yet bitten production because nxeon-web's systemd unit still runs
# `npm start` (next start) today, not server.js directly — but this fix must
# land before that switch happens, not after.
if [ -d node_modules/geoip-lite/data ]; then
  mkdir -p .next/standalone/node_modules/geoip-lite/data
  cp -r node_modules/geoip-lite/data/. .next/standalone/node_modules/geoip-lite/data/
fi
# Web runs as the unprivileged 'nxeon' user. .next needs to be writable by it
# (Next cache); the rest stays root-owned and world-readable. .env is the one
# exception: systemd's EnvironmentFile= reads it as root (PID 1, pre-privilege
# drop) so the app's process env is fine either way, but Prisma's generated
# client ALSO opens .env directly at Client instantiation to resolve its own
# env() directives — that read happens as the actual 'nxeon' process user, so
# a root-owned .env throws EACCES there on every cold start (harmless once
# systemd's injected vars are already in process.env, but noisy, and a prior
# root-run edit to this file silently reverted the ownership fix below once
# already — confirmed live 2026-09-02). Keep .env nxeon-owned, not world- or
# group-readable. Do NOT chown the whole tree (breaks root git on .git).
echo "==> Fixing .next/.env ownership for non-root web"
chown -R nxeon:nxeon /opt/nxeon/.next 2>/dev/null || true
chown nxeon:nxeon /opt/nxeon/.env 2>/dev/null || true
chmod 600 /opt/nxeon/.env 2>/dev/null || true
echo "==> Restarting production web"
systemctl restart nxeon-web

# Drain in-flight provisions before bouncing the worker. Restarting the worker
# mid-provision used to interrupt a live VM build and (with a non-idempotent retry)
# strand the server in ERROR. The start step is now idempotent so this is
# belt-and-suspenders, but avoiding the interruption entirely is cleaner. Bounded
# wait (max ~4 min) so a deploy can never hang forever.
DBURL=$(grep -E '^DATABASE_URL=' /opt/nxeon/.env | head -1 | cut -d= -f2- | tr -d '"')
if [ -n "$DBURL" ] && command -v psql >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  for _ in $(seq 1 24); do
    ACTIVE=$(psql "$DBURL" -tAc "SELECT count(*) FROM \"Job\" WHERE status='RUNNING' AND type='PROVISION';" 2>/dev/null | tr -d '[:space:]')
    [ "${ACTIVE:-0}" = "0" ] && break
    echo "==> Waiting for ${ACTIVE} in-flight provision(s) to finish before restarting worker…"
    sleep 10
  done
fi

echo "==> Restarting production worker"
systemctl restart nxeon-worker
sleep 5
systemctl is-active nxeon-web nxeon-worker
CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://127.0.0.1/)
echo "==> Production responds: HTTP $CODE"
[ "$CODE" = "200" ] || { echo "PRODUCTION UNHEALTHY — check journalctl -u nxeon-web"; exit 1; }
echo "==> Production promote complete"
